title: Bipartisan Fury Mounts as Trump Abruptly Shelves Mandated Russia Sanctions
snippet: Lawmakers from both parties are blasting President Donald Trump's decision to indefinitely suspend sanctions on Moscow, accusing the administration of capitulating to Vladimir Putin ahead of the midterm elections.
content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump ignited a fierce bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill Saturday after suddenly waiving major economic sanctions against Russia just days before they were scheduled to go into effect.

The sanctions, codified under the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act, were passed by an overwhelming 86-11 vote in the Senate as a direct response to Moscow's ongoing invasion of Ukraine. However, late Friday, Trump issued an executive order putting the measures on hold indefinitely, citing national security concerns. The move comes on the heels of a controversial diesel import agreement Trump struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin—a long-shot bid to drive down skyrocketing pump prices that are weighing heavily on voters ahead of the November midterms.

'Beyond Irresponsible'

The executive action drew swift condemnation from key leaders on both sides of the political aisle, who accused the White House of overriding the explicit will of Congress.

"Beyond irresponsible," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., posted on social media. "What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine." Tillis added that if the administration wanted to tackle energy costs, it should address the conflict with Iran rather than "doing a solid for Vladimir Putin."

Democrats echoed the outrage. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York declared that "by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier," while Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., warned that the president was "enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression."

Legislative Roadblocks and Midterm Politics

Opponents face steep hurdles in counteracting the executive order. Both the House and Senate are currently on recess until after the upcoming elections, leaving Capitol Hill virtually powerless to mount an immediate legislative response.

Despite the recess, Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced legislation aiming to block the U.S.-Russia diesel deal, calling the arrangement "corrupt" and inconsistent with American principles. "At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine," Meeks said.

The decision also places a spotlight on South Carolina, where Darline Graham—appointed to fill the Senate seat of her late brother, Lindsey Graham—is locked in a tight election fight. Speaking at a campaign event, Graham expressed her preference for maintaining sanctions. "Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia," she said, though she acknowledged that she and the president sometimes "agree to disagree."

Meanwhile, officials in Kyiv expressed deep disappointment over the stall, warning that Ukraine faces a harsh winter as Russian forces continue targeting its critical energy infrastructure.
